summary: Describes DASS, the Distributed Authentication Security Service, an experimental design for proving who users and services are in a distributed environment, aiming to be both more secure and easier to use than existing mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary:
DASS is a design for proving your identity across a network without sending your password around. Each user and each machine has a key pair, and a certification authority signs a certificate that binds a name to the public half.

When two parties authenticate, they exchange an authentication token that carries a shared session key and a timestamp, so that a captured token cannot be used again later.

questions: how does dass use certification authorities
how does dass prevent replay attacks
what is the distributed authentication security service
how does dass provide mutual authentication
subtitle: A protocol for proving who you are across a network, using public keys instead of passwords.

tldr.problem: Passwords do not work well in a distributed network: a password typed at one machine tells nothing about the same user at another, and passwords can be picked up by anyone listening on the wire.
tldr.mechanism: DASS gives every user and machine a public and a private key. A certification authority signs a certificate binding a name to a public key, and an authentication token carries a ticket, a shared DES key and a timestamped authenticator.
tldr.outcome: The result is strong mutual authentication and a global identity that any node in the network recognises. The document is Experimental and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 1507 is an Experimental document from September 1993 and has not been obsoleted. It defines DASS as a component of the Distributed System Security Architecture, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are discussed throughout the memo.

sections.title: What DASS Is For
sections.content:
Authentication is a security service, and the goal of authentication is to reliably learn the name of the originator of a message or request. The classic way people authenticate to computers, and computers to one another, is by supplying a password. DASS tries to solve the problems with existing password-based schemes by providing authentication services in a distributed environment that are both more secure, in that it is more difficult for a bad guy to impersonate a good guy, and easier to use than existing mechanisms.

Authentication is particularly challenging in a distributed environment. Users do not simply log on to one machine and use resources there; they start processes on one machine which may request services on another, and in some cases the second system must request services from a third system on behalf of the user. Given current network technology, it is fairly easy to eavesdrop on conversations between computers and pick up any passwords that might be going by.

DASS uses cryptographic mechanisms to provide strong, mutual authentication. Mutual authentication means that the two parties communicating each reliably learn the name of the other. Strong authentication means that in the exchange neither obtains any information that it could use to impersonate the other to a third party. This cannot be done with passwords alone. Mutual authentication can be done with passwords by having a sign and a counter-sign which the two parties must utter to assure one another of their identities, but whichever party speaks first reveals information which can be used by the second, unauthenticated party to impersonate it. Longer sequences cannot solve the problem in general, and anyone who can eavesdrop on the conversation can impersonate either party in a subsequent conversation unless passwords are only good once. Cryptography provides a means whereby one can prove knowledge of a secret without revealing it.

People cannot execute cryptographic algorithms in their heads, and so cannot strongly authenticate to computers directly. DASS lays the groundwork for smart cards, microcomputers sealed in credit cards which, when activated by a PIN, will strongly authenticate to a computer. Until smart cards are available, the first link from a user to a DASS node remains vulnerable to eavesdropping, and DASS mechanisms are constructed so that after the initial authentication, smart card based and password based authentication look the same.

Today, systems think of user identities in terms of accounts on individual computers. If a user has accounts on ten machines, there is no way in advance to see that those ten accounts belong to the same individual, and to access a resource through any of the ten machines the user must tell the resource about all ten accounts, and must also tell it when an eleventh account appears. DASS supports the concept of global identity and network login: a user is assigned a name from a global namespace and that name is recognised by any node in the network. From a practical point of view a user can have a single password or smart card usable on all systems which allow access, and access control mechanisms can conveniently give access to a user through any computer the user happens to be logged in to. Because a single user secret is good on all systems, it should never be necessary to enter a password other than at the initial login, and because cryptographic mechanisms are used, the password should never appear on the network beyond the initial login node.

DASS was designed as a component of the Distributed System Security Architecture. It is a goal of that architecture that access control on all systems be based on users' global names, and that the concept of accounts on computers eventually be replaced with unnamed rights to execute processes on those computers. Until that happens, computers will continue to support local accounts, and the Berkeley rtools database that gives access to local accounts from remote accounts is envisioned as being extended to grant access based on DASS global names, which would simplify the administration of those databases for the common case where a user should be granted access to an account ignoring his choice of intermediate systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is not only proving who you are, it is proving who you are once, in a way that every machine you use can check. DASS gives you one name that travels, and one secret that never has to travel after the first login.

sections.title: Public Keys, Timestamps and Delegation
sections.content:
DASS makes heavy use of the RSA public key cryptosystem. The properties that matter are that it supports the creation of a public and private key pair, where operations with one key reverse the operations of the other but it is computationally infeasible to derive the private key from the public key; that it supports signing a message with the private key, after which anyone knowing the public key can verify the signature and know that it was made with knowledge of the private key and that the message was not subsequently altered; and that it supports enciphering a message by anyone knowing the public key such that only someone with knowledge of the private key can recover the message. With those, a strong authentication mechanism is easy to see: each principal, user or computer, would construct a key pair, publish the public key and keep the private key secret. To authenticate to you, I would write a message, sign it with my private key and send it to you; you would verify it with my public key. The algorithms DASS actually uses are considerably more complex, to deal with a large number of practical concerns including subtle security threats.

On replay protection, DASS uses the timestamp-based scheme rather than challenge and response. In a challenge and response scheme the verifier generates a challenge, the claimant includes it in the signed message, and the verifier accepts the message only if it contains the recently generated challenge, never issuing the same challenge twice. In the timestamp scheme the claimant includes the current time, and the verifier will not accept messages more than, say, five minutes old and keeps track of all the messages it has seen in the last five minutes, so a replay inside the window is rejected because the message is remembered, and a replay after the window is rejected as timed out. The disadvantage of challenge and response is that it requires extra messages, always at least three, where one-way authentication could be done with a single message. The disadvantage of the timestamp scheme is that it requires secure synchronised time, because if clocks drift apart by more than five minutes the verifier rejects every attempt to authenticate, and if a time service spoofer can turn a clock back and then replay an expired message it will be accepted again. The timestamp scheme also requires the server to keep state about all messages seen in the clock skew interval, which for security must be kept on stable storage. DASS chose timestamps so that authentication messages could be piggybacked on existing connection establishment messages and so that DASS would fit within the same form factor, number and direction of messages, as Kerberos.

On delegation, when a user logs onto a computer the user wants to prove identity to that computer and also to use it to access network resources on their own behalf. Their files should be protected so that they can be accessed through any node they log in through, without allowing all of the systems they might ever use to access those files in their absence. In the process of logging in, the user's password gives the login node access to the user's RSA secret, which it can use to impersonate the user on any request it makes on the user's behalf, and it should forget all secrets associated with the user at log off. When a user accesses a network service, they want to strongly authenticate to it without letting it learn anything that would allow it to impersonate them; when using some services, such as remote login, the user may want the service to act on their behalf in calling additional services, and DASS provides a mechanism for passing secrets that allow them to do so. This version can limit delegation only in terms of time: the information a user gives a server other than the initial login node can be used to impersonate the user, but only for a limited period.
sections.plainLanguage: DASS signs messages with a private key that only the user holds, and adds the time so that a captured message cannot be replayed later. A user can also hand a server a limited pass to act on their behalf.

sections.title: Certification Authorities and Their Hierarchy
sections.content:
On certification authorities, the flaw in the simple strong authentication mechanism is that it assumes every principal knows the public key of every other principal it wants to authenticate to. A certification authority is a principal trusted to act as an introduction service: each principal goes to the authority, presents its public key and proves it has a particular name, and the authority creates a certificate containing the name and public key of the principal, an expiration date and bookkeeping information, signed by the authority's private key. All subscribers to a particular authority can then authenticate to one another by presenting their certificates and proving knowledge of the corresponding secret. The two problems with this are revocation and scaleability.

Revocation is the process of announcing that a key has, or may have, fallen into the wrong hands and should no longer be accepted as proof of a particular identity; someone who learns your secret and certificate can otherwise impersonate you indefinitely. DASS supports two independent mechanisms. The first uses timeouts and renewals: part of the signed certificate is a time after which it should not be believed, and the authority periodically renews certificates by signing one with a later timeout, so a compromised key gets a new key and a new certificate while the old one stays valid only until its timeout. Timeouts are not perfect, because they give only slow revocation and depend on servers having an accurate source of the current time. The second method lists all non-revoked certificates in the naming service and believes only those found there; it is almost immediate, but the availability of authentication is then only as good as the availability of the naming service, and the security of revocation only as good as the security of the naming service. A third method, revocation lists issued periodically by the authorities, is not currently supported.

Using a certification authority as an introduction service scales much better than having every principal learn the public key of every other by some out-of-band means, but it creates a central point of trust: the authority can impersonate any principal by inventing a new key and certifying it. DASS addresses this by creating a hierarchy of certification authorities tied to the naming hierarchy. For each directory in the namespace there is a single authority responsible for certifying the public keys of its members, and that authority also certifies the public keys of the authorities of all child directories and of the parent directory. With this cross-certification, knowing the public key of any authority lets a verifier check a series of intermediate authorities and finally the public key of any principal. Because the hierarchy is tied to the naming hierarchy, the trust placed in any individual authority is limited: a compromised authority can impersonate any of the principals listed in its directory, but not arbitrary principals, and a compromise low in the naming tree compromises all principals below that directory while a compromise high in the tree compromises only principals far apart in the hierarchy, so when multiple organisations share a namespace the compromise of an authority in one organisation cannot result in false authentication within another.

DASS uses the X.500 directory hierarchy for principal naming, with country names at the top. National authorities are not expected to establish certification authorities, at least initially, so an alternative mechanism is used to authenticate entities distant in the naming hierarchy: the cross-certificate, where an authority certifies the public key of some authority or principal that is neither its parent nor its child. By limiting the chains used to parent certificates followed by a single cross-certificate followed by child certificates, an implementation can avoid the need to have authorities near the root of the tree, or avoid the requirement to trust them even if they exist.

On user against node authentication, DASS supports the mutual authentication of two principals regardless of whether they are people, computers or applications, and extends those mechanisms to the common case of a user and a node authenticating together to a single remote server, by optionally having two sets of secrets in each credential structure, one for the user and one for the node, so that both secrets sign the request. The security of such a setup is less, because a node can impersonate all of its users even when they are not logged in, but it offers an easier transition from existing global identities for all users.

On protection of user keys, DASS deals mainly with authentication between principals each knowing a private key, but for people special mechanisms are provided. It is often most convenient to keep passwords as secrets rather than private keys, and the architecture specifies a means of storing private keys encrypted under passwords. This would give security as good as hiding a private key were it not that people tend to choose passwords from a small space, such as words in a dictionary. To address that weakness, DASS specifies a protocol between a login node and a login agent whereby the login agent can audit and limit the rate of password guesses. Use of these features is optional: a user with a smart card could store a private key directly and bypass all of these mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A certification authority signs a certificate that binds a name to a public key, and the authorities are arranged in a tree that matches the tree of names. Checking a key means walking up the tree to a common ancestor and back down.

sections.title: An Authentication Walkthrough
sections.content:
The OSI Authentication Framework characterizes authentication as occurring in six phases, and the RFC describes DASS in those terms. In the installation phase, principal certificates are created along with the additional information needed to create claimant and verifier credentials, and OSI defines three sub-phases. Enrollment is the definition of a principal in terms of a key, name and UID. Validation is confirmation of identity to the satisfaction of the authority, after which the authority generates a certificate. Confirmation is the act of providing the user with the certificate and with the authority's own name, key and UID, followed by the user creating a trusted authority for that authority, which is a certificate for the authority signed by the user. Posting the certificate so that it is available to principals wishing to verify the principal's identity is part of this step, and the user principal saves the trusted authority for use when it creates credentials.

In the distribution phase, DASS distributes certificates by placing them in the name service. In the acquisition phase, whenever principals wish to authenticate to one another they access the name service to obtain whatever public key certificates they need and create the necessary credentials. Claimant credentials implement the representation of a principal in a process, and in making this representation the principal delegates to a temporary delegation key, so that the claimant's long term principal key need not remain in the system. Claimant credentials are made by invoking the get credentials primitive, and contain a name; a ticket, which holds a validity interval, a UID, the temporary delegation public key and a digital signature over those made with the principal's private key; and the delegation private key. There may also be credential information relating to the node on which the user is logged in and the account on that node. Verifier credentials are made with initialize_server and consist of a principal long term private key, because these credentials are usually needed by servers that must run indefinitely without re-entry of any long term key. Claimants and verifiers also have a trusted authority, which consists of the name of the trusted authority, which appears in the issuer field in principal certificates, its public key, used to verify certificates it issues, and its UID. Trusted authorities are used to verify certificates for other principals' public keys. The authorities are arranged in a hierarchy corresponding to the naming hierarchy, where each directory is controlled by a single authority, and each authority certifies the authority of its parent directory, the authorities of each of its child directories, and optionally authorities elsewhere in the naming hierarchy. Even though a principal has only a single trusted authority, it can securely obtain the public key of any principal in the namespace by walking the hierarchy.

In the transfer phase, the claimant sends an authentication token to the verifier. Tokens are made by invoking the create_token primitive and are cryptographically protected and specified as a DASS data structure in ASN.1. The authentication token includes the ticket; a DES authenticating key encrypted using the intended verifier's public key, and with it one of two things, either a digital signature on the encrypted DES key made with the delegation private key when delegation is not being performed, or the delegation private key DES encrypted using the DES authenticating key when delegation is being performed; and an authenticator, which is a cryptographic checksum made with the DES authenticating key over a buffer containing a timestamp and any application supplied channel bindings, such as addresses or other context information, whose purpose is to thwart substitution and replay attacks. There may also be optional information about node authentication and context. As a side effect, after init_authentication_context the caller receives a local authentication context, a data structure holding the DES key and, if mutual authentication is being requested, the expected response. To construct the token the claimant needs the verifier's public key certificate, which it gets from the name service.

An authenticator can only be used once, but it is permissible to re-establish the same local authentication context multiple times, since the ticket and DES key establishment components may have a relatively long lifetime. That allows a performance improvement, because repeated public key operations can be alleviated by caching authentication contexts along with other components of a successfully used token and the associated verified principal public key; creating and verifying fresh authenticators based on a cached authentication context is a relatively inexpensive operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates are put in a directory service, and the two parties pick them up from there. The claimant wraps a session key for the verifier with the verifier's public key and adds a timestamped checksum, so the verifier can be sure the token is fresh and meant for it.

sections.title: Certificates and Authentication Tokens
sections.content:
A certificate is a data structure posted in the naming service which proclaims that knowledge of the private key associated with a stated public key authenticates a named principal. Certificates are signed by some authority, are readable by anyone, and can be verified by anyone knowing the public key of the authority. DASS organises the authority trust hierarchy around the naming hierarchy: there is a trusted authority associated with each directory, and generally each authority creates certificates stating the public keys of each of its children and the public key of its parent, so that anyone knowing the public key of any authority can learn the public key of any other by walking the tree. In order that principals may authenticate even when all of their ancestor directories do not participate in DASS, authorities may also create cross-certificates, which certify the public key of a named entity that is not a descendant.

The syntax and content of DASS certificates are defined in terms of X.509, and DASS considers certificates to be of one of six types. Normal Principal certificates are signed by an authority and certify the name and public key of a principal, where the name of the authority is a prefix of the name of the principal and is one component shorter. Trusted Authority certificates are signed by an ordinary principal and certify the name and public key of the principal's authority. Child certificates are signed by an authority and certify the name and public key of an authority of a descendant directory. Parent certificates are signed by an authority and certify the name and public key of the authority of its parent directory. Cross certificates are signed by an authority and certify the name and public key of an authority of a directory where neither name is a prefix of the other. Self certificates are signed by a principal or an authority and the issuer and subject names are the same; they are not used in this version of the architecture but are defined as a convenient data structure in which implementations may insecurely pass public keys, and may be used in the future in certain key roll-over procedures.

The parts of a certificate used by the algorithms are the UID of the issuer, which is optional; the full name of the issuer, being the authority or principal signing; the UID of the subject, also optional; the full name of the subject, the authority or principal whose key is being certified; the public key of the subject; the period of validity, with an effective date and an expiration date; and the signature over the entire content of the certificate.

The authentication token passed from client to server is complex, with a large number of optional parts, while the token passed from server to client, in the case of mutual authentication only, is small and simple. The authentication process begins when the initiator calls Create_token with the name of the target, which returns a token that is sent to the target; the target calls Accept_token with it, and both routines produce a second mutual authentication token that the target returns to the initiator to prove it received the first. The initial token contains an encrypted shared key, which is a shared DES key encrypted under the public key of the target, with a validity interval and a recognizable pattern included in the encrypted structure so the receiver can tell whether decryption succeeded; a login ticket, which is a delegation certificate signed by a principal's long term private key delegating to a short term public key, whose active ingredients are the UID of the delegating principal, the period of validity, the delegation public key, and a signature made with the private key of the principal, whose existence is testimony that the private key corresponding to the delegation public key speaks for the user during the validity interval; and a shared key ticket, a signature of the encrypted shared key made with the delegation public key in the login ticket, whose existence is testimony that the DES key in the encrypted shared key speaks for the user.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six kinds of certificate, differing only in who signed them and whose name they cover. The token that travels from the user to the server holds the session key, wrapped so only the server can open it, plus a ticket and a timestamp.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of RFC 1507 says only that security issues are discussed throughout the memo, and they are: the choice of the timestamp scheme and its dependence on synchronised time, the two revocation mechanisms and their trade-offs, the rules governing what a compromised authority can and cannot impersonate, and the weakness of passwords as a store for private keys.

The memo also sets out the security requirements it places on the services it uses. For detecting the replay of authentication tokens, the system needs access to a strictly monotonic time source which is reasonably synchronised across the network, within a few minutes, for the system to work; inaccuracy does not present a security threat except in one scenario, where a client whose clock is made sufficiently fast has its tokens rejected and someone harvesting those tokens from the wire can replay them later and impersonate the client. For aging stale entries from caches, DASS requires reasonably accurate timing of intervals.

For generating keys, DASS needs a source of cryptographic quality random numbers, meaning that knowing any of the random numbers returned from a series and knowing all state information which is not protected, an attacker cannot predict any of the other numbers in the series. Hardware sources are ideal. A 56-bit truly random seed, for example from a series of coin tosses, could be used as a DES key to encrypt an infinite length known text block in CBC mode to produce a pseudo-random sequence, provided the key and the current point in the sequence were adequately protected.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is unusual in that its security discussion is spread through the whole document rather than collected at the end. The main risks it names are clock skew, weak passwords and random numbers of poor quality.

messages.label: Request for the verifier's certificate
messages.note: The claimant needs the verifier's public key to encrypt the shared DES key.

messages.label: Certificate
messages.note: The certificate binds the verifier's name to its public key.

messages.label: Authentication token
messages.note: Carries the ticket, the DES authenticating key encrypted under the verifier's public key, and the authenticator.

messages.label: Mutual authentication token
messages.note: Proves the verifier received the token, for mutual authentication.

viz.caption: The central concepts of DASS (RFC 1507, Section 1.2)

items.title: Strong and mutual authentication
items.text: Both parties learn the other's name, and neither learns anything that would let it impersonate the other to a third party.

items.title: Timestamps rather than challenges
items.text: DASS uses the timestamp-based scheme, so authentication messages can be piggybacked on connection establishment and the message flow matches Kerberos.

items.title: Delegation
items.text: A user hands a server a secret that lets it act on their behalf, valid only for a limited time.

items.title: A hierarchy of authorities
items.text: Each directory in the naming hierarchy has one authority, which certifies its children's and its parent's public keys, so a chain can be walked.

items.title: Revocation
items.text: Two mechanisms: certificates expire and are renewed, or the naming service lists the certificates that are still valid.

items.title: User and node credentials together
items.text: A credential can carry a secret for the user and one for the node, so that both must sign the request.

viz.caption: The six DASS certificate types (RFC 1507, Section 3.1)

items.label: Signed by an authority
items.desc: Certifies the name and public key of a principal.

items.label: Signed by a principal
items.desc: Certifies the name and public key of that principal's own authority.

items.label: Signed by an authority
items.desc: Certifies the name and public key of an authority of a descendant directory.

items.label: Signed by an authority
items.desc: Certifies the name and public key of the authority of its parent directory.

items.label: Signed by an authority
items.desc: Certifies the name and public key of an authority of a directory where neither name is a prefix of the other.

items.label: Signed by a principal or authority
items.desc: The issuer and subject names are the same. Not used in this version of the architecture.
